In this homework/lab we will explore the normal distribution along with percentiles. To help demonstrate the ideas and draw the distributions we will make use of the following function without giving full details.

Below some examples,

plot_normal(0,1)

Question 1 - Normal Distribution and Percentiles

Suppose that SAT scores are normally distributed with mean 1100 and standard deviation 200 and ACT scores are normally distributed with mean 21 and standard deviation 6.

Written symbolically,

SAT ~ N(1100,200) ACT ~ N(21,6)

Visually each distribution,

# SAT
plot_normal(1100,200)

# ACT
plot_normal(21,6)

part a)

Alex scored 1300 on his SAT. His percentile can be visualized by the light blue area under the curve.

plot_normal(1100,200,0,1300)

Or calculated directly,

pnorm(1300,1100,200)
## [1] 0.8413447

The interpretation: Alex scored better than 84% of all SAT test takers.

part b)

The standard normal distribution is specifically a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

z-scores follow the standard normal distribution.

z = (observation - mean ) / (standard deviation)

z-score can be thought of as the number of standard deviations away from the mean.

Alex scored 1300 on his SAT which is normally distributed with mean 1100 and sd 200.

z_alex <- (1300 - 1100) / 200
print(z_alex)
## [1] 1

The interpretation: Alex scored one standard deviation above the mean.

part c)

The z-score is a standardization or transformation. The results/percentiles will be identical.

Previously: A score of 1300 from N(1100,200) Standardized: A score of 1 from N(0,1)

plot_normal(1100,200,0,1300) # (mean, sd, left_bound, right_bound)

plot_normal(0,1,-9,1)

pnorm(1300,1100,200) # (observation, mean, sd)
## [1] 0.8413447
pnorm(1,0,1)
## [1] 0.8413447

part d)

Bob scored a 30 on his ACT. Calculate his z-score and percentile.

#(ANSWER)
z_bob <- (30-21) / 6
z_bob
## [1] 1.5
pnorm(30, 21, 6)
## [1] 0.9331928

part e)

Interpret Bob’s z-score and percentile.

(ANSWER) BoB scored 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. Bob scored better than 93% of all ACT test takers.

part f)

Alex scored a 1300 from N(1100,200). Bob scored a 30 from N(21,6).

Who scored better? Why?

(ANSWER) Bob scored in the 93rd percentile and Alex scored in the 84th percentile, so Bob scored better overall.

Question 2 - Inverse Normal Distribution

Consider the same normal exam distributions as before

SAT ~ N(1100,200) ACT ~ N(21,6)

In question 1 we calculated percentiles using the function pnorm.

pnorm input: observation output: percentile

Consider now, the inverse function

qnorm input: percentile output: observation (quantile or x value)

This is known as the inverse normal distribution.

Carl is applying for college and needs to score in the top 10% on his SAT. What score does he need?

part a)

To begin this question we should first consider the distribution.

plot_normal(1100,200)

We are interested in the top 10% but we don’t know where the bounds should go.

# Where does the bound go SUCH THAT we have 10% area on the right.

plot_normal(1100,200,1300,5000)

plot_normal(1100,200,1400,5000)

plot_normal(1100,200,1500,5000)

part b)

WANT: the score / the observation / the quantile / the x value

The score associated with the top 10% is the same score associated with the bottom 90%.

plot_normal(1100,200,0,1300)

plot_normal(1100,200,0,1400)

plot_normal(1100,200,0,1500)

REMEMBER: By definition, all percentiles are calculated as the area on the left.

part c)

Use qnorm() function now to calculate the score.

(carl_needed_score <- qnorm(0.90, mean = 1100, sd = 200))
## [1] 1356.31

Visualize the given percentile and associated score.

plot_normal(mean = 1100, sd = 200, 0, carl_needed_score)

part d)

Suppose that Carl also needs to score in the top 2.5% on his ACT. What score does he need? Use the qnorm() function.

#(ANSWER)
qnorm(0.975, mean = 21, sd = 6)
## [1] 32.75978

part e)

We can double check our previous answer using the 68-95-99.7 rule.

Recall that,

Within one standard deviation of the mean, there is 68% of the data.

plot_normal(21,6,21-6,21+6)

Within two standard deviations of the mean, there is 95% of the data.

plot_normal(21,6,21-12,21+12)

Within three standard deviations of the mean, there is 99.7% of the data.

plot_normal(21,6,21-18,21+18)

If there is 95% of the data within two standard deviations from the mean, then, how much of the data is outside that range? 5%.

Also remember that the normal distribution is symmetric.

If there is 5% of the data in the left and right tails combined, then, there is 2.5% of the data in each tail.

By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what score is associated with the top 2.5%?

(ANSWER) 33, which is 2 standard deviations above the mean

Submission

Once you have completed all the questions, submit your compiled document as a pdf on Canvas. There are several ways to compile and/or convert to a pdf, perhaps the most straightforward way to do so would be as below,

  1. knit to html (shortcut ctrl + shift + k, or near the top left)
  2. open in browser (near the top left)
  3. print to pdf (depending on your browser this may be different)

If you prefer a more savvy solution you can print to pdf directly from R studio. However, pdf output requires you to setup and install TeX (MiKTeX on Windows, MaxTeX on OS X, TeX Live on Linux). The installation of TeX is a bit more involved so it will not be required and/or covered.
